To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we developed computational methods to extract, analyze, and integrate spatial information from electron microscopy of nanometer-scale electron probes on cell membranes and that we applied these methods to study the spatial organization and dynamics of signaling pathways in cells.

the topography of signaling molecules and receptors can be determined by the spatial patterns of nanometer-scale electron probes on the cell membrane, and that these patterns can be analyzed to determine the topography of the molecules.
the topography of signaling molecules can be mapped at high resolution using electron microscopy and nanometer-scale probes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the topography of cell signaling molecules, and the development of computational methods for the analysis and modeling of spatial data obtained from electron microscopy.
the characterization of the topology of cell membrane receptors and signaling complexes using nanometer scale electron dense probes and electron microscopy.
developing new approaches to map and analyze the spatial distributions of proteins and lipids within cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the methods described here are useful in the study of the spatial distribution of proteins in cell membranes, and in the study of their interactions with each other.

the use of the methods and tools described herein will allow the user to extract the spatial distribution of probes in a membrane sheet and to statistically validate the clustering of probes and to integrate these results between experiments in a way that is appropriate for the analysis of the spatiotemporally regulated interactions of proteins and lipids during cell signaling.

the combination of nanometer-scale electron microscopy and computer-assisted image analysis provides a powerful new approach to characterize the spatial organization and interactions of signaling proteins, lipids and other molecules in the cell membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a method for mapping the topography of signaling components on the cytoplasmic membrane surface and for characterizing the spatial relationships between them.
we have developed a high-resolution approach for the spatiatemporal analysis of cell signaling networks, which we have validated using the well-known model for cell signaling, the EGF receptor.
the methods we describe provide a powerful approach to characterize the topology of cell signaling networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of electron microscopy with computational tools for spatial analysis can be used to obtain quantitative information about the organization of signaling proteins in the cell membrane.
the analysis of electron micrographs of membrane sheets can be carried out in a systematic way to provide information about the topography of signaling molecules in the cell membrane.
it provides the means to analyze and model the spatial organization of signaling components at a nanometer scale and with high spatial resolution.
